Why did NASA launch a seventy-seven-year-old senator into Earth orbit?

title: Why NASA Sent a 77-Year-Old to Orbit
description: In 1998, John Glenn returned to orbit aboard Space Shuttle Discovery at age seventy-seven. While critics called it a publicity stunt, the flight yielded vital research on aging.

beats.text: Most people thought NASA sent a seventy-seven-year-old into orbit for publicity.
beats.visual: official portrait of John Glenn in orange launch suit for STS-95, 1998
queries: John Glenn orange flight suit STS-95

beats.text: In 1998, thirty-six years after flying Friendship 7, sitting senator John Glenn boarded shuttle Discovery.
beats.visual: Space Shuttle Discovery standing on launch pad 39B before STS-95, 1998

beats.text: With President Bill Clinton watching the launch, drama struck at ignition when a drag chute door fell off.
beats.visual: President Bill Clinton watching the launch of STS-95 through binoculars, 1998

beats.text: Critics dismissed the mission as political hype, but Discovery carried over eighty science experiments.
beats.visual: interior of the pressurized Spacehab module aboard Space Shuttle Discovery, 1998

beats.text: Researchers specifically designed tests to study how spaceflight mimics the human aging process.
beats.visual: astronaut John Glenn performing scientific procedures inside Spacehab on STS-95, 1998

beats.text: Glenn served as a test subject, providing seventeen blood and forty-eight urine samples during flight.
beats.visual: medical equipment and sample collection kits used aboard STS-95, 1998
queries: John Glenn STS-95 sleep and blood study

beats.text: He logged 134 orbits and remains the oldest person ever to reach Earth orbit.
beats.visual: Space Shuttle Discovery descending toward the runway at Kennedy Space Center, 1998

beats.text: His flight delivered rigorous research on aging, even though skeptics still spread a very different story.
beats.visual: John Glenn smiling after egress following the landing of STS-95, 1998
